headline: In New Orleans, Carnival and festivals get the money before the Pelicans do
summary: This is a high-tourism, moderate-income market. People dress for parades, second lines, tailgates and festivals, and heat and humidity rule most of the year. Locals watch the price tag, while visitors pay more for anything city-specific. Team gear rides on Zion Williamson, Trey Murphy III and the City Edition, not on winning.

insights.title: Carnival is the first-quarter peak
insights.detail: Carnival runs from Twelfth Night (Jan 6) to Mardi Gras Day, which falls on Feb 9 in 2027. In the weeks before, locals buy purple, green and gold gear, throw-related items and parade-day outfits. The Pelicans' home calendar competes with parade routes, and many fans plan around krewe schedules.
insights.implication: Have a Carnival-adjacent capsule ready by mid-January, not February. Keep it about the city's wardrobe (hoodies, tees, caps), not literal throws or krewe marks.

insights.title: Light layers, with a short winter
insights.detail: Summers are hot and humid, hurricane season runs June to November, and rain is frequent year-round. Genuine cold lasts a few weeks between December and February. Fans buy shorts and breathable tees far longer than in northern markets, then add a hoodie or light jacket for cold snaps and over-air-conditioned arenas.
insights.implication: Weight assortments toward lightweight tees, shorts, quarter-zips and water-resistant shells. Keep outerwear thin, packable and rain-ready, not heavy puffer.

insights.title: Festivals outrank the NBA calendar for spend
insights.detail: Four events pull big shopper crowds that overlap with the NBA offseason or the start of fall. Essence Festival of Culture runs over July 4 weekend. Jazz Fest runs late April into early May. The Bayou Classic (Grambling vs Southern in the Superdome) takes Thanksgiving weekend, and Southern Decadence takes Labor Day weekend. Essence brings a national Black audience with real spending power.
insights.implication: Plan pop-ups and city-product drops around Essence and the Bayou Classic. They reach locals and out-of-town buyers when the Pelicans aren't playing. Partner with HBCU and Black-owned local voices.

insights.title: Sunday second lines drive local social commerce
insights.detail: Social aid and pleasure clubs parade most Sundays from roughly September to May in custom-dyed matching outfits. The outfits, suits, fans and sneakers are commissioned and photographed heavily on Instagram. Mardi Gras Indian culture keeps a parallel, craft-based season, with Super Sunday in March and St. Joseph's night around March 19.
insights.implication: Treat second-line fashion as a custom, color-matched, sneaker-forward market. Offer coordinated team colorways and customization, and hire the clubs as paid collaborators instead of borrowing their imagery.

insights.title: Price-sensitive locals, bigger-spending visitors
insights.detail: Orleans Parish has a large lower-income population and a hospitality workforce paid in tips. Cash flow follows tourist seasons, tax-refund season and Carnival work. Visitors buy a premium souvenir piece, and often a jersey, on a trip.
insights.implication: Tier the range. Offer accessible swingman, kids and tees for local households, and a premium city-keepsake tier and authentic pieces for visitors and out-of-state Pelicans fans.

insights.title: The Pelicans compete with Saints, LSU and Tulane
insights.detail: Football (Saints, LSU in Baton Rouge, Tulane) and the Sugar Bowl on New Year's Day set the fall and winter fan calendar. Pelicans gear is often the second or third team purchase. Sentiment is cool: the team went 26-56, its second straight sub-30-win season, and had a quiet offseason with no 2026 first-round pick.
insights.implication: Lead with Zion, Trey Murphy III, Derik Queen, Jeremiah Fears and the City Edition, not the standings. Use Cup nights and the new-coach story for early-season hooks.

places.name: Smoothie King Center
places.why: The home arena and main in-person team-gear spot on game nights, next to the Superdome.

places.name: Caesars Superdome
places.why: Hosts Saints games, the Sugar Bowl and the Bayou Classic, the city's biggest fall and winter apparel-buying crowds.

places.name: Canal Street
places.neighborhood: Central Business District / French Quarter edge
places.why: The historic retail spine and main Carnival parade route, where visitors and locals converge.

places.name: Magazine Street
places.why: A long strip of local boutiques and streetwear-adjacent shops serving affluent locals and visitors.

places.name: Riverwalk Outlets
places.why: Tourist-heavy outlet shopping beside the convention center and cruise terminal.

places.name: Lakeside Shopping Center
places.why: The main suburban mall for Jefferson Parish families, and a major mainstream sneaker and team-gear channel.

places.name: Oakwood Center
places.why: Anchors West Bank family shopping, apart from the east-bank tourist economy.

places.name: Congo Square, Louis Armstrong Park
places.why: A historic gathering ground whose Sunday and festival culture is central to Black New Orleans identity. Approach it through community partners.

people.name: Zion Williamson
people.why: The franchise's biggest jersey and sneaker draw, and the likeliest driver of national sales, not just local.

people.name: Trey Murphy III
people.why: A breakout scorer averaging 21.5 ppg last season, and a rising second jersey name despite June trade rumors.

people.name: Derik Queen and Jeremiah Fears
people.why: Next-wave names for kids and youth product, and for telling the young-core story.

people.name: Jamahl Mosley
people.why: The new-era story for the early-season marketing window.

people.name: Big Freedia
people.role: Bounce music artist from New Orleans
people.why: The best-known bounce ambassador, a natural voice for a high-energy, local-first collaboration if approached respectfully and paid.

people.name: Trombone Shorty
people.why: A widely respected local figure tied to Jazz Fest, second-line music and the city's youth music programs.

people.name: Essence Festival of Culture (Essence Communications)
people.why: Brings a national Black audience to the city every July and is a major retail and brand stage.

moments.name: Twelfth Night / Carnival kickoff
moments.why: The start of the season for parade outfits, king cakes and purple-green-gold buying.

moments.name: Sugar Bowl
moments.why: College football crowds and holiday-week visitor spending around the Superdome.

moments.name: Mardi Gras Day
moments.why: The peak of the Carnival wardrobe and the city's biggest tourism week.

moments.name: Super Sunday and St. Joseph's Night
moments.why: Mardi Gras Indian showcase days. It is a ceremonial and craft tradition, so don't borrow from it without the culture bearers.

moments.name: New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival
moments.why: A large visitor and local festival crowd, and a major merchandise moment.

moments.name: Essence Festival of Culture
moments.why: A national Black audience, with fashion and brand events across the city.

moments.name: Southern Decadence
moments.why: A large LGBTQ+ gathering in the French Quarter and Marigny that drives tourist spending.

moments.name: Bayou Classic
moments.why: The Grambling vs Southern HBCU rivalry, with major tailgate, band and fashion culture and heavy apparel buying.

productHooks: A Carnival-season capsule (tees, hoodies, caps) in purple, green and gold accents with Pelicans navy, ready by mid-January.
A lightweight Louisiana-weather range in team colors: breathable tee, short and packable rain shell for year-round wear.
A matched-set drop (tee, short, cap) designed with local second-line and streetwear voices, with revenue shared.
An Essence and Bayou Classic weekend pop-up with city-only graphics and numbered small runs for visitors.
Value-tier Zion, Trey Murphy III and kids' swingman and tee bundles for family and holiday gift buying.
watchouts: Mardi Gras Indian suits, patches and ceremonial imagery are sacred craft traditions. Don't reproduce them. Engage the culture bearers, credit them and pay them.
Saints marks, 'Who Dat' and krewe names carry licensing or ownership concerns. Confirm rights before use.
Second-line and social aid and pleasure club identities belong to specific Black communities. Partner with them, don't lift from them.
Avoid caricature of Bourbon Street party imagery. Locals prefer neighborhood-rooted references.
Hurricane season (June to November) can disrupt event, shipping and retail timing.

channels.role: Game-night impulse buying, and the main place visitors buy a Pelicans jersey.
Metairie and West Bank malls and sporting-goods chains are the main route for families and kids.
Local shops on Magazine Street and in neighborhoods carry the culture-driven, limited product.
Second-line fashion, local designers and custom outfits are found and sold through social media.
Essence, Jazz Fest and Bayou Classic vendors capture dense visitor spend.
Out-of-town fans and sneaker buyers shop online and in resale for Zion product and City Edition pieces.

extra.priceProfile: Orleans Parish is lower-income with a high poverty rate, alongside an affluent Uptown and Garden District. Household cash flow is tied to tips and seasonal hospitality work. Locals respond to accessible prices, bundles and kids' value tiers. Visitors will pay for a premium or limited city-specific piece. Louisiana's combined state and Orleans local sales tax is roughly 10 percent as of 2025, and there is no standing back-to-school tax holiday. Read price tags as all-in at checkout.
extra.jerseyBehavior: Local fans lean toward swingman jerseys and tees at lower prices, and kids' jerseys are the big gift item. Committed fans and visitors buy most of the authentic jerseys. Zion Williamson is the leading name, with Trey Murphy III rising, and the City Edition is the big limited moment. Knockoffs and unlicensed festival-vendor shirts are part of the local streetwear economy and set the price anchor for official product.
